case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause requires that a State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may permanently terminate parental rights, and New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional.
key_cases.relevance: This is the federal constitutional floor that Rhode Island's Family Court applies in every termination case under R.I. Gen. Laws § 15-7-7, and it is the standard the Rhode Island Supreme Court enforces on review.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination, reiterating that a finding of parental unfitness is a mandatory predicate that must precede any termination of parental rights.
key_cases.relevance: This is the cleanest Rhode Island statement of the unfitness-first rule: best interests never substitute for a finding of unfitness in a termination case.
key_cases.quote: A trial justice must make a finding of unfitness before she may terminate a parent's rights.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed where DCYF developed four case plans tailored to the mother's issues and the Family Court correctly concluded the department satisfied its statutory reasonable-efforts obligation notwithstanding her non-compliance.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion ties the reasonable-efforts finding directly to the § 15-7-7(a)(3) twelve-month and substantial-probability analysis.
key_cases.quote: we are of the opinion that the Family Court justice correctly concluded that DCYF complied with its statutory obligation to make reasonable efforts to reunify respondent with Violet

key_cases.holding: On remand after the earlier vacatur, termination was affirmed; the Court restated that findings in a termination proceeding must rest on clear and convincing evidence and upheld admission of the child's statements to her therapist under Rule 803(4).
key_cases.relevance: It is the current Rhode Island Supreme Court statement of the burden of proof and standard of review in termination appeals.
key_cases.quote: Such findings must be supported by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed on the abandonment ground because the father, who had the Family Court and DCYF addresses and was represented by counsel elsewhere, failed to maintain contact, so the Court did not need to reach the alternative unfitness ground.
key_cases.relevance: Malachii O. is the modern Rhode Island statement of the abandonment ground and confirms that one sustained statutory ground is enough to affirm.
key_cases.quote: Because we are of the opinion that the Family Court justice correctly concluded that respondent abandoned his son, we need not address § 15-7-7(a)(2)(i) as an additional basis for termination.

key_cases.holding: The termination decree was vacated and remanded for a hearing with proper notice because the record did not show compliance with § 15-7-9, which requires a sworn affidavit of the absent parent's last known whereabouts before notice by publication may be ordered.
key_cases.relevance: Joziah B. makes § 15-7-9 notice a strict prerequisite to any Rhode Island termination against an absent parent.
key_cases.quote: Our examination of the record, however, reveals a fatal flaw in this case which constrains us to vacate the termination decree.

key_cases.holding: Both termination decrees were vacated: DCYF failed to make reasonable efforts as to the mother because it never offered substance-abuse treatment for what it identified as her primary barrier to reunification, and the father's unfitness was never proved by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: Steven D. is the standard Rhode Island citation for the unfitness-first, clear-and-convincing rule, and it shows the Court vacating a decree where the trial justice made no unfitness findings at all as to one parent.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that, before the state may terminate a parent's rights in his or her children, the state must support its allegations by clear and convincing evidence
